title: The Universal Scam Checklist
intro: Scams change their costume constantly. The machinery underneath almost never does. Nearly every scam needs at least three of the six things below, and the more of them you can tick, the closer you are to certainty. You do not need to recognise the specific scam. You only need to recognise the shape.

pillars.name: 1. Who started this?
pillars.detail: Almost every scam begins with contact you did not initiate: a message, a call, a DM, an ad, a wrong number, a stranger at an ATM. When you go looking for a service, you control where you land. When it comes to you, someone else chose the moment, the framing and the story.
checks: Did this reach me unprompted, rather than me seeking it out?
Am I using contact details that came from the message itself?
Did the conversation move quickly to a private channel like WhatsApp?
Did a stranger introduce me to this opportunity, platform or person?

pillars.name: 2. Why must this happen right now?
pillars.principle: Urgency is manufactured to stop you thinking.
pillars.detail: Time pressure is the most reliable single marker of fraud. Reversing a fraudulent payment in ten minutes. Securing the flat today. Releasing the prize before it lapses. Genuine institutions have processes, records and patience. Fraud needs you to act before you check, because checking is all it takes to defeat it.
checks: Is there a deadline, countdown or threat of immediate loss?
Am I being discouraged from hanging up, leaving, or thinking it over?
Would waiting 24 hours genuinely cost me anything real?
Am I being told to keep this confidential, or not to discuss it with family?

pillars.name: 3. How am I being asked to pay?
pillars.principle: Irreversible payment methods are chosen deliberately.
pillars.detail: Criminals steer you to payment channels that cannot be reversed: EFT to a personal account, e-wallet, cash, gift cards, crypto. This is not a preference, it is a requirement of the business model. Card payments and regulated gateways create a dispute route, which is exactly what they are avoiding.
checks: Am I being asked for an EFT to a personal account, e-wallet, cash, gift cards or crypto?
Does the account name match the business I think I am dealing with?
Am I being asked to pay a fee to receive money, a prize, a refund, a loan or my own funds?
Am I being asked to move money to a 'safe' or 'holding' account?

pillars.name: 4. What are they asking me to reveal or install?
pillars.principle: Nobody legitimate needs your OTP, PIN or your screen.
pillars.detail: There is no situation, ever, in which a bank, retailer, courier, government department or employer needs your one-time PIN, your card PIN, your password, or remote access to your device. Not to verify you. Not to help you. Not to stop a fraud. This one rule, held absolutely, closes the majority of attacks.
checks: Am I being asked for an OTP, PIN, password or full card number?
Am I being asked to forward a verification code I received?
Am I being asked to install AnyDesk, TeamViewer or any remote access tool?
Am I being asked for ID documents, a selfie holding my ID, or bank statements?

pillars.name: 5. Can I verify this on a channel they did not give me?
pillars.principle: Verification only counts if you choose the channel.
pillars.detail: Every detail presented to you can be forged: caller ID, sender IDs, letterheads, logos, websites, review counts, video of a person's face, the voice of your own child. None of it is evidence. The only meaningful test is independent contact, using a number or address you already had or found yourself, on a different channel from the one they reached you on.
checks: Can I hang up and call back on a number from my card, my statement or the official website?
Have I checked the licence or registration myself, on the regulator's own site?
Have I reverse image searched the photographs?
Am I trusting caller ID, an SMS thread, a logo or a padlock icon as if it were proof?

pillars.name: 6. Does the money make sense?
pillars.principle: Ask where the profit actually comes from, and insist on an answer.
pillars.detail: Every offer implies a flow of money. A legitimate one can explain it in a sentence that survives a follow-up question. Guaranteed high returns, prices far below every other seller, a job with no interview, a stranger's generosity: each requires someone to be losing money for your benefit. Ask who, and why they would.
checks: Can I explain in one sentence where the profit or the discount comes from?
Does this require someone to act against their own interest for my benefit?
Is the return guaranteed, fixed, or unusually smooth?
Does earning depend on me recruiting other people?

hardRules: No bank, ever, asks for your OTP, PIN or password. There is no exception and no emergency that creates one.
There is no such thing as a safe account, a holding account or a suspense account you must move your money into.
You never pay a fee to receive money. Not a prize, not a refund, not a loan, not an inheritance, not your own investment profits.
You never pay to be given a job.
Never forward a verification code to anyone, including someone who appears to be a close friend.
Never install remote access software because an inbound caller asked you to.
Never send money to someone you have not met in person.
Any change of banking details, on any invoice, from anyone, is verified by voice call on a number you already had.
Caller ID, sender IDs, logos, https padlocks and five-star reviews are all trivially faked. None of them is verification.
Anyone who contacts you offering to recover money you have already lost is scamming you again.

thirtySecondTest.detail: Say out loud that you are not deciding anything in the next ten minutes. The pressure is the attack, and naming it defuses it.
Close the message. Do not click the link, do not call the number in it, do not reply.
Use the number on your bank card, your statement, or the official website you navigate to yourself.
Where exactly does the money come from, or, can you confirm this reference from your side without me telling you what it is?
Say it out loud to somebody. Scams rely on isolation, and most of them fall apart the moment they are described to a third party.
